items.title: Early Edition: October 22, 2026
items.excerpt: A curated weekday guide to major news and developments over the last 24 hours. Here’s today’s news: IRAN WAR Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy today said four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by Iranian forces yesterday. The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the U.S. military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. Tala Ramadan reports for Reuters. The U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the U.S. midterms, U.S. officials and other sources told the New York Times. The countries’ militaries have stepped up exercises, flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers. The strikes would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal. Julian E. Barnes, Eric Schmitt, Farnaz Fassihi, Natan Odenheimer, and Ronen Bergman report. Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets on Monday conducted a sortie, flying as far as the Iranian border, Israeli and U.S. officials told Axios. The operation took place on the same day U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but wasn’t connected to Hegseth’s visit. Barak Ravid reports. IRAN WAR – YEMEN Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation yesterday blamed the Iran-aligned Houthis for a new attack on the eastern Saudi city of Dammam’s airport which killed two people and injured another eight. The U.S. State Department said it ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their families from the kingdom in response to increased hostilities against Saudi Arabia by the Houthis. David Gritten reports for BBC News; James T. Areddy and Abeer Ayyoub report for the Wall Street Journal. IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS ... New York Democrat congressional candidate Brad Lander yesterday said he was briefly detained and released by the Israeli military while he was supporting Palestinian farmers during an olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. The New Israel Fund said approximately 90 volunteers of what they’re calling the Protect the Harvest initiative were released. Two Israeli lawyers told NPR it was the largest mass detention of activists in the occupied West Bank in at least a decade. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said Lander’s actions amounted to “political provocation,” and noted that he chose to enter a restricted area and participate in an unauthorized activity without coordinating with local authorities. Joseph De Avila reports for the Wall Street Journal; Ruth Sherlock, Samantha Balaban, Nuha Musleh, and Daniel Estrin report. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff yesterday called Russian President Vladimir Putin a “humanitarian” following the release of U.S. citizen Stephen James Hubbard from Russian custody. In a meeting between the pair, Putin told Witkoff that he “agrees in principle” to resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States to end the war in Ukraine, Russian and U.S. officials told Axios. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he hoped the three-way talks will be held as soon as possible, preferably no later than early November. David E. Sanger, Kim Barker, and Ivan Nechepurenko report for the New York Times; Barak Ravid reports; Ron Popeski reports for Reuters. Ukraine’s Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko yesterday said a Russian missile attack was launched at Ukraine’s capital, injuring six people. The attack came hours after Putin said he was “ready in principle” to resume peace talks and after Trump said the world was “the closest we’ve been” to ending the war. Russia said Ukraine launched 630 drones towards its capital Moscow overnight. Jaroslav Lukiv reports for BBC News; Olena Harmash and Gleb Bryanski report for Reuters. ... The U.N. World Meteorological Organization yesterday said the El Niño weather pattern could cause a record rise in ocean temperatures in the Pacific as it barrels across the world like a “wrecking ball,” causing floods and droughts. The WMO’s seasonal outlook predicted the El Niño event would become extremely strong and cause temperatures to rise by 3.8 degrees Celsius. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said “we have not seen in our records 3.8. We have seen around 3 in some record El Niños before, with very substantive impacts across the world.” Olivia Le Poidevin reports for Reuters. ... CEO of global connectivity and internet security company Cloudflare Matthew Prince yesterday said the company saw thousands of attempts to exploit a flaw AI identified 10 hours before global hacks were publicly announced. Developers of the PHP programming language released urgent new fixes to vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years until they were uncovered by AI. Government officials across the world are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack. Sam Sabin reports for Axios; Raphael Satter, Leo Marchandon, Kanjyik Ghosh, and Rajveer Pardesi report for Reuters. Company executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file workers to trust AI over their own judgement, according to a survey from Charter published yesterday. Charter in August surveyed 5,002 U.S. office workers at companies with at least 100 employees who said they use AI at work. 32.8% of executives said they trust AI more than their own judgement, while only 16.3% of other workers said the same. Emily Peck reports for Axios. ... New Mexico yesterday filed a civil lawsuit against sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime lawyer and accountant, Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn, accusing the pair of helping finance and conceal Epstein’s sex trafficking at his remote Zorro Ranch property in Stanley, New Mexico. The suit alleges several Jane Does, including minors, were abused at the ranch, and Indyke arranged payments to victims that left them indebted to Epstein, while Kahn monitored the spending of victims and even prepared tax returns for some. Khadeeja Safdar reports for the Wall Street Journal. A New Mexico judge yesterday ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties after a jury in September found that the company misled users about their data privacy. The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke. New Mexico is the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled with Meta. Josephine Walker reports for Axios.

items.title: US inflation rose slightly last month after 2 years of steady cooling but remained low
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON (AP) — Inflation in the United States ticked up in October, driven by costlier rents, used cars and air fares, a sign that price increases might be leveling off after having slowed in September to their lowest pace since 2021. ... Consumer prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 2.4% in September. It was the first rise in annual inflation in seven months. From September to October, prices edged up 0.2%, the same as the previous month. Excluding volatile food and energy costs, “core” prices rose 3.3% from a year earlier, the same as in September. From September to October, core prices rose 0.3% for a third straight month. Over the long run, core inflation at that pace would exceed the Fed’s 2% target. ... An uptick in prices, if sustained, could stir concerns in financial markets that progress in taming inflation may be slowing. It might also make the Federal Reserve less inclined to cut its key interest rate in the coming months, as its officials have previously indicated they likely would. ... Still, most economists think inflation will eventually resume its slowdown. Consumer inflation, which peaked at 9.1% in 2022, has since fallen steadily, though overall prices are still about 20% higher than they were three years ago. ... At a news conference last week, Fed Chair Jerome Powell expressed confidence that inflation is still heading down to the central bank’s 2% target, though perhaps slowly and unevenly. ... A survey released Tuesday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that consumers expect prices to rise just 2.9% in the next 12 months, which would be the lowest such measure in nearly four years. Lower inflation expectations are important because when consumers expect milder price increases, they’re less likely to act in ways that raise inflation, such as accelerating their purchases or demanding higher pay to offset higher prices. ... Another potential source of relief for Americans’ budgets is in apartment rents. They are now barely rising on average nationwide, according to the real estate brokerage Redfin. Its measure of median rent was just 0.2% higher than it was a year ago in October, at $1,619, though that figure reflects rents only for new leases.

items.title: US Leading Indicators
items.excerpt: The Conference Board Leading Economic Index® (LEI) for the US was unchanged in September 2026 at 99.6 (2016=100), after a decline of 0.1% in August. The LEI grew by 0.6% between March and September 2026, a reversal from its decline of 1.1% over the previous six months (September 2025 to March 2026). ... “The US LEI was flat in September. However, due to an upward revision to July’s data, the Index is at a higher level than last month’s report for August,” said Justyna Zabinska-La Monica, Senior Manager, Business Cycle Indicators, at The Conference Board. “Five out of ten components made positive contributions to the LEI in September, led by the interest rate spread and average weekly hours in manufacturing. Nevertheless, these gains were offset by a large decline in consumer expectations and much smaller negative contributions from stock prices, new orders for capital goods and building permits. The LEI’s six-month growth rate increased slightly, which suggests the economy is still growing and will continue to grow, but is becoming less dependent on consumer spending and more dependent on business investment. The Conference Board now expects real GDP to grow by a 2.2% annualized rate in 2026, with our outlook for 2027 at 2.0%, higher than previously forecasted.” ... The Conference Board Coincident Economic Index® (CEI) for the US increased by 0.3% in September 2026 to 115.3 (2016=100), following a 0.1% increase in August. Overall, the CEI rose by 0.9% over the six months between March and September 2026, up from its 0.2% growth over the previous six months. The CEI’s four component indicators—payroll employment, personal income less transfer payments, manufacturing and trade sales, and industrial production—are included among the data used to determine recessions in the US. items.title: Market sell-off gains steam on Iran war, high AI spending fears
items.excerpt: U.S. equity markets sold off sharply Thursday, as fears that Israel and the United States would restart attacks against Iran sent oil prices higher and major tech stocks failed to hold on to recent gains. The S&P 500 was down 1.3% by 2 p.m. ET, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen 2.5%. The price of international Brent crude climbed nearly 4%, while U.S. crude gained 2.5%. Demand for Treasury bonds also increased — bucking the trend of the last several months — as investors sought out the safe-haven assets as riskier ones like tech stocks sold off. That sent the 10-year yield below 5% for the first time since late September.

Paweł Pawlikowski, master of the 90-minute movie, returns with 'Fatherland' NEW YORK (AP) — Storytelling economy can be in short supply at the movies. But Paweł Pawlikowski has made a career out of a concision that now seems almost radical. His last three films — “Ida,” “Cold War” and his latest, “Fatherland” — are all 90 minutes or less. Each is shot in black and white, in a boxy academy ratio. And none has a single ounce of fat on it. In an era where three-hour movies are commonplace, the 69-year-old Polish filmmaker has refined a style of less is more. His movies are brief but unhurried, lean yet profound. “Fatherland,” starring Sandra Hüller, opens in select theaters Friday. ... Movie Review: In ‘Fatherland,’ Paweł Pawlikowski’s austere portrait of a fractured Germany Filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski explores family and country in his new film “Fatherland.” Inspired by Thomas Mann's 1949 return to Germany, the film delves into themes of exile and identity. It follows Thomas, played by Hanns Zischler, and his daughter, played by Sandra Hüller, on a trip from West Germany to East Germany after many years away. In her review, Associated Press Film Writer Lindsey Bahr writes that Pawlikowski's film is painterly and profound, a brisk and somber indictment of the idea of postwar optimism that fits neatly in his unofficial trilogy with “Ida” and “Cold War.” “Fatherland” opens in select theaters Friday. Tom Cruise to receive life achievement award from the American Film Institute LOS ANGELES (AP) — Tom Cruise is being honored with a life achievement award from the American Film Institute. AFI's board of trustees announced Wednesday that the award will be presented at a gala tribute in Los Angeles next April. Kathleen Kennedy, chair of AFI's board, praised Cruise as a global icon and highlighted his dedication to film. Cruise, 64, has starred in numerous films over four decades, earning three Academy Award nominations. He also received an honorary Oscar last year. The AFI Life Achievement Award recognizes individuals whose work has advanced film and stood the test of time. ... Movie Review: 'Clayface' arrives as a pretty good R-rated revenge thriller-horror romance DC Studios has turned to an unlikely character for its next feature movie, says AP critic Mark Kennedy. “Clayface,” directed by James Watkins, is a revenge thriller-romance and body-horror origin story for a lesser-known Batman villain. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Matt Hagen, a rising actor whose life changes after a mobster disfigures him. He turns to a scientist, played by Naomi Ackie, for help. The film explores themes of identity and Hollywood's obsession with beauty. Kennedy says that despite being Batman-less, "Clayface" is a crowd-pleaser with practical effects and biting satire. The R-rated movie hits theaters Friday.
